U.S. officials enacted 50% duties on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods on August 22, 2026, triggering Canada's retaliation after trade negotiations collapsed over the weekend.

Ottawa unveiled a C$7.5 billion financial support package alongside the counter-tariffs, offering interest-free loans and extended employment insurance to protect workers and businesses affected by the trade dispute.
President Donald Trump escalated tensions on Truth Social, suggesting he might rename Lake Ontario 'Lake America' and calling Canada 'the most difficult and unreasonable' nation to deal with.
Trump threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts to 50% starting January 1, 2027, further pressuring the integrated auto sector amid the escalating trade war.

Maxwell, a British socialite, was convicted in 2021 for recruiting and grooming young women for Jeffrey Epstein, who died by suicide in 2019 before his own trial.
Claiming a 'complete miscarriage of justice,' Maxwell argued that new evidence from the Justice Department proved her rights were violated at trial and sentencing.
Engelmayer rejected the arguments, calling them 'lengthy and rambling' and noting her assertions were based on 'speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods' instead of credible facts.
The judge ruled that alleged 'new' evidence from the Justice Department's Epstein files is 'largely irrelevant' to her case, stating no fact 'fairly puts in dispute' the trial outcome.
title: Federal judge rejects Ghislaine Maxwell’s ‘miscarriage of justice’ claim and bid for prison release

Lancaster remains the center of a major measles outbreak that has sickened nearly 400 people across 28 Pennsylvania counties this year, with children comprising about one-third of cases.
The MMR vaccine provides 97% lifetime protection against measles, yet health officials noted that none of the patients diagnosed this year in Pennsylvania were fully vaccinated.
Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen warned that measles can cause serious complications including pneumonia and brain swelling, while expressing sympathy for the affected families.
Pennsylvania reports the third-highest number of measles cases in the U.S. for 2026, while the World Health Organization states that about 95% community vaccination is required for herd immunity.
title: Pennsylvania reports two deaths from measles, health department says

Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade negotiations last Friday, prompting Trump to impose 50% tariffs on approximately $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.
Escalating the dispute on Monday, Trump threatened new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles and steel while demanding leaders "fall in line" or face consequences "far WORSE."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut electricity and critical mineral exports, stating "everything is on the table" if the dispute worsens.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued on Monday that Canada's auto industry relies on the 1960s Auto Pact, while Carney accused Washington of attempting to dismantle Canadian sectors.
title: Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, official tells AP

summary: On Monday, the Supreme Court cleared the way for President Donald Trump to move ahead with his executive order restricting mail-in voting, though it remains unclear how much his administration can implement before the midterm elections.

Signed in March, President Trump's executive order directs the federal government to compile lists of eligible voters and orders The Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists.
Under the new rules, States must submit voter lists to The Postal Service for every mail ballot, with each ballot tied to a unique barcode containing the voter's name and home address.

Lawyers from Democratic-run States sued to block the order, arguing President Trump lacks authority to change election regulations, while a federal judge in Boston froze the directive pending the Supreme Court's final action.
title: Supreme Court clears the way for Trump mail voting order in advance of midterms

summary: On Tuesday, August 25, 2026, South Carolina Republican voters returned to polls for a Senate runoff between Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman to determine the party's nominee for the November general election.

Following the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham in July, Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham to finish the term; no candidate secured an outright majority in the August 11 special primary, triggering this runoff.
Campaign resources have poured into the race, with President Donald Trump spending more than $827,000 for Graham and former governor Nikki Haley's aligned PACs contributing over $700,000 for Norman.
During a recent debate, Graham admitted she was "not that informed on national security" regarding Taiwan, which Norman, a five-term congressman, leveraged to emphasize his legislative experience.
Whoever wins the runoff will face Democrat Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in the November general election for a seat considered a safe Republican hold.
title: Sen. Darline Graham wins the Republican Senate primary runoff in South Carolina

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani stated Tuesday he opposes the rally, though he acknowledged the city lacks legal jurisdiction to cancel the private event scheduled for August 29.

summary: Retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. successfully advanced from Alaska 's top-four nonpartisan primary to the general election, alongside Republican incumbent U.S. Senator Dan S. Sullivan.
The incumbent's campaign and Republican allies had previously tried to block the challenger from the ballot, accusing him of being a "sham candidate" brought in to confuse voters.
The Alaska Supreme Court ultimately ruled in favor of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., allowing his name to remain on the primary and general election ballots.
To minimize voter confusion, state election officials listed the incumbent on ballots with his full title and registration while designating the challenger as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr."
Both Sullivans will move on to the November ranked-choice general election, joining leading Democratic candidate and former U.S. Representative Mary Peltola.
title: Republican with same name as incumbent Dan Sullivan advances from Alaska US Senate primary

Eyewitness video from January 24 shows Pretti recording when an officer shoved a woman into him; officers then removed his legal firearm while he was on the ground before approximately 10 shots were fired.

President Donald Trump called Pretti an "agitator" and "insurrectionist" after confrontation footage surfaced 11 days before the shooting; the killing occurred during "Operation Metro Surge," roughly two weeks after ICE officer shot Renee Good.

Attorney Steve Schleicher told ABC News that a July 13 meeting with the U.S. Attorney "raised more questions than answers." The Department of Justice opened a federal civil rights investigation into the shooting.

Micayla Pretti demanded the agents' names be officially released, while her mother Susan Pretti stated, "They murdered our child," emphasizing the family's right to be consulted meaningfully throughout the investigation.
title: Alex Pretti’s family calls for accountability 7 months after fatal CBP shooting

Voter sentiment shifted after President Donald Trump launched the war on Iran in February, pushing gasoline prices near record highs and straining U.S. household finances.
The survey of 951 registered voters found 36% favor the Democratic Party approach, 28% picked Republicans, and 37% remain unsure or believe neither party has a viable plan.
White House spokesperson Kush Desai cited "historic job, wage, and economic growth" in defense, while Republican strategist Christopher Nicholas warned Republicans face exposure on cost of living.
With the entire House and 35 Senate seats up for grabs in November, Republicans aim to highlight tax cuts while framing the Democratic Party as increasingly extreme.
title: Democrats up 7 points on the economy over GOP: Poll

Trump set normalization as a condition for the deal to take effect, citing the Abraham Accords reached in 2020 and 2021 between Israel and nations including the UAE and Bahrain.

Saudi Arabia has demanded an irreversible path to a Palestinian state, as normalization efforts stalled following the start of Israel's war on Gaza in October 2023.
title: Trump has submitted civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia to Congress for review, AP sources say

President Donald Trump justifies the attacks as "armed conflict" against cartels; the latest incident brings the total killed in 68 strikes to at least 227 people.

Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International condemn the strikes as extrajudicial killings, while Washington maintains operations target "narco-terrorists" operating along established Caribbean routes.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently discussed expanding joint military operations against criminal groups onto land in Colombia, Guatemala, and Honduras, signaling potential strategy shift.
title: US Military Says It Killed Four in Strike on Alleged Drug-Smuggling Boat in the Caribbean

Detention followed the July 7 shooting, which ICE labeled a 'targeted enforcement operation,' while officials claimed the driver, Salgado Araujo, had 'weaponized his vehicle' and officers fired in self-defense.

Passengers disputed the account, stating agents struck their van from behind; Judge Bennett ruled Pantoja has 'no criminal history, is not a flight risk, and does not otherwise pose a danger to the community.'
Following the release of Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego last month, Pantoja is the second witness freed, though Victor Hugo Salgado Araujo remains detained in Conroe.

Federal prosecutors are expected to appeal the release, having previously cited 5th Circuit cases to justify mandatory detention, as the Trump administration continues to seek deportation for the men.
title: Another witness ordered released after a fatal shooting by a federal immigration agent in Texas

summary: United States Capitol Police arrested a man on Tuesday after spotting a guillotine in his pickup truck parked near the Capitol Building and Supreme Court building.
Invented in late-18th-century France, the guillotine consists of a heavy blade mounted on a wooden frame and became a symbol of the Reign of Terror during the French Revolution.
Officers detained 35-year-old Philan-Tam-Duy of Julian, California, shortly after 3 p.m. when his truck was found illegally parked in the 100 block of East Capitol Street.
Police charged Philan-Tam-Duy with Carrying a Dangerous Weapon, and USCP investigators are examining why he drove from California to the District and his intent behind transporting the device.
Investigators are currently reviewing the driver's background to determine why he made the trip to the Capitol and what motivated him to transport the device.
title: Police Arrest a California Man After Finding a Guillotine Near the US Capitol

Mike Mazzei was endorsed by President Donald Trump and outgoing Governor Kevin Stitt, who opposes Gentner Drummond and supports Mazzei as a pro-business candidate.

This lawsuit follows a wave of litigation alleging technology companies designed platforms to hook children; Sunday filed similar action against TikTok earlier this month, with Snap, Google, TikTok, and Meta collectively facing more than 3,000 lawsuits.

Prosecutors allege features like infinite scroll and Snapstreaks drive behavioral addiction by keeping minors on the platform to view a "never-ending stream of content," creating pressure to maintain friendships through daily communication.

Pennsylvania seeks civil penalties and injunctions requiring Snapchat to update app store ratings and implement youth safety measures, while Snap disputed the allegations, maintaining its platform features strong protections for teens.

Sunday continues collaborating with legislators on consumer privacy legislation and remains engaged in multi-state litigation against Meta, positioning this enforcement action within a broader pattern of tech-industry oversight.
title: Pennsylvania attorney general accuses Snapchat of failing to protect children in new lawsuit

summary: On Monday, Tampa International Airport officials announced they will maintain federal Transportation Security Administration screening operations, rejecting the proposed TSA Gold+ privatization program after a months-long review.
Earlier this year, the TSA approached TPA with Gold+, a public-private partnership program designed to improve operational resilience through private contractor screening under federal oversight.

AFGE National President Everett Kelley praised the decision, stating "Tampa airport officials made the right call," while Tampa Bay-area Democratic U.S. Rep. Kathy Castor had urged TPA to reverse privatization plans.

The Transportation Security Administration is replacing Gold+ with an evolved Screening Partnership Program as part of Administrator David Cummins' Horizon 25 Strategy to modernize checkpoints and elevate traveler experience.

Charleston International Airport and Des Moines International Airport also announced Gold+ plans last month, but neither provided updates on their decisions as of Monday afternoon, leaving their privatization status uncertain.
title: Tampa airport axes plan to staff TSA checkpoints with private workforce

summary: On Aug. 24, 2026, The Florida Department of Health proposed a rule to remove four immunizations from PreK-12 school entry requirements, targeting Hepatitis B, varicella, Haemophilus influenza type b, and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines.

State Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo has pursued eliminating vaccine mandates for nearly a year, with Gov. Ron DeSantis joining him Last September to call on the Florida Legislature to roll back all state vaccine mandates.

The proposed rule expands religious vaccine exemptions to include moral and ethical beliefs, and permits parents and college students to opt out of having their vaccination records included in the state vaccine database.

American Academy of Pediatrics President Susan Kressly warned the policy puts children at risk, while Panama City pediatrician Eehab Kenawy said removing mandates sends a message that "vaccines are not important, vaccines are not needed."
Following Ladapo's approval of the rule on Aug. 20, 2026, the department opened a 21-day public comment period before final approval takes effect.
title: Florida moves to end certain school vaccination requirements

Before his 2022 Senate election, Avila served eight years in the Florida House of Representatives, rising to Speaker Pro Tempore, and currently serves as a captain in the Florida Army National Guard.

Currently chairing the Senate Finance and Tax Committee, Avila sponsored property tax relief measures exempting up to $250,000 of primary home values and the Stop WOKE Act, positioning the ticket to prioritize lowering costs for families.

Democratic nominee David Jolly congratulated the selection but argued the race centers on Donalds' close political alliance with President Donald Trump rather than on the running mate choice in the November general election.
The selection gives Donalds deep political ties to Miami-Dade and the influential Cuban-American community, strengthening outreach to Hispanic voters as the campaign builds momentum toward November.
title: Donalds picks state senator as running mate for Florida governor

summary: On Monday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the New York City Office of the Chief Medical Examiner announced the first 9/11 victim identification using forensic investigative genetic genealogy, marking the first identification in almost 12 months.

Approximately 2,753 people died in the 2001 attacks, yet 1,099 victims—40 percent of those killed—remain unidentified nearly 25 years after the tragedy, spurring forensic scientists to continue testing remains.

Forensic investigative genetic genealogy pairs specialized DNA sequencing with genealogical research to build family trees, allowing researchers to narrow potential identities from millions of possibilities to specific leads.
Medical Examiner Dr. Jason Graham called FIGG a "promising new addition" to their toolkit, emphasizing the office's commitment to identifying victims and providing families with closure and clarity.
This breakthrough marks the 1,654th victim identified, offering hope as the city prepares to commemorate the 25th anniversary at the National September 11 Memorial on Friday, September 11, 2026.
title: 9/11 Victim Identified Nearly 25 Years Later Through Breakthrough New Technique, Officials Say

The Texas Republican emphasized he would "certainly be part of the discussion" regarding the party's ideological direction, explicitly leaving his own electoral future open for 2028.
title: Cruz says GOP hasn’t coalesced behind Vance for 2028 nomination: ‘Oh, no’

summary: N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, a 31-year-old nurse and member of the Chickasaw Nation, won the Democratic Senate primary runoff in Oklahoma against Jim Priest despite being heavily outspent.

Thomas identifies as a democratic socialist who supports progressive policies such as Medicare for All, universal childcare, parental leave, and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement but does not support defunding the Defense Department.
Thomas will face GOP Representative Kevin Hern in the general election, who has a significant financial advantage and is favored to win in the heavily Republican state.
Thomas's campaign spent significantly less than her opponents, with $57,000 in the primary and only $456 on hand for the general election, compared to Hern's $2.6 million as of June 30.
title: N’Kiyla Thomas wins Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Oklahoma

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds Blair’s Democratic identity and his “defeats” of a late congressman’s daughter, framing the runoff as a partisan setback and family succession story.

Right-Leaning framing sharpens the dynastic angle—“House Dem,” “father’s term,” and “fell short”—while also spotlighting Blair as a “historic candidate,” the first Black openly gay man elected to Congress from Georgia.

summary: On Tuesday, Former Gwinnett County School Board Chair Everton Blair won Georgia's 13th Congressional District special election runoff, securing 52.46% of the vote to fill the remainder of the late Rep. David Scott's term.
The runoff followed a July 28 special election where five candidates competed; because no contender reached a 50% majority, Blair and Democrat Marcye Scott advanced to face each other.
According to the Secretary of State's Office, Blair defeated Scott by fewer than 800 votes in a district spanning six counties and nearly 800,000 residents across the Atlanta metro area.
Blair will serve only through early January and is not running in November's general election, where Democrat Jasmine Clark and Republican Jonathan Chavez will compete for a full term.

The vacancy arose after Rep. Scott died in April following more than two decades representing the district, prompting the special election to ensure Georgia's 13th had representation through the remainder of his term.
title: Democrat Everton Blair defeats Rep. David Scott’s daughter in the special election for the late congressman’s seat

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the episode as an “expanding” Trump-linked “leak” probe, using “criminal investigation,” “walked out,” and “do not admit” to suggest escalating institutional secrecy, while right-leaning coverage intensifies the scandal narrative with “rocked,” “criminal leak probe,” and “hit with” orders, portraying the Secret Service as engulfed in turmoil.
Their pivotal divide is whether leaks and possible classified information define the case or remain unconfirmed allegations.

summary: On Tuesday, the Secret Service placed three officials on administrative leave amid an Office of Professional Responsibility investigation into suspected classified leaks to the media.
Journalist Susan Crabtree reported the FBI and CIA are involved in the criminal inquiry, with the suspended personnel designated as "do not admits" as part of the investigation.
CNN identified one suspended official as communications chief Anthony Guglielmi, while all three officials lost their security clearances and the other two worked in communications.

It remains unclear if the leaks pertain to controversy over President Trump's secret evacuation from Turkey due to intelligence about a surface-to-air missile threat to Air Force One from Iran, Crabtree noted.

Federal enforcement efforts have increasingly targeted unauthorized disclosures, including The DOJ's subpoenas of New York Times journalists and digital device seizures from Max Blumenthal, plus a previous Secret Service inquiry regarding Vice President Vance.
title: 3 Secret Service officials placed on leave amid misconduct investigation

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the $21.5 million payment as the price of Trump’s “ DEI crackdown,” using “cost” and “consequences” to portray punitive government pressure on companies.

Right-Leaning coverage instead emphasizes an investigation into allegedly “discriminatory practices,” Deloitte’s denial, the affirmative-action claimant group, and $4.3 million in planned distribution, presenting settlement as nonadmission; “targeted” underscores perceived governmental pressure.
Center coverage largely de-emphasizes ideological judgment, sticking to “settle” and “probe” while noting the policy shift.
The pivotal divide is whether the case signals anti-DEI overreach or accountability for disputed practices, though all acknowledge DOJ involvement, the $21.5 million figure, and Trump-era scrutiny.
summary: On Tuesday, accounting firm Deloitte agreed to pay $21.5 million to settle a U.S. Department of Justice probe into its diversity, equity and inclusion practices.

The Justice Department reached the settlement through its "Civil Rights Fraud Initiative," alleging Deloitte business units tracked "demographic goals" and evaluated Partners, Principals and Managing Directors on workforce composition.
Under the False Claims Act, the American Alliance for Equal Rights, founded by Edward Blum, will receive $4.3 million as part of the settlement resolving whistleblower claims.
Deloitte denied engaging in discriminatory conduct, stating the agreement does not amount to an admission of liability, as the company sought to avoid protracted litigation costs.

President Donald Trump's administration has targeted DEI practices during his second term, with executive orders requesting federal contractors eliminate such initiatives, prompting many U.S. companies to scale back.
title: Deloitte to pay $21.5 million to settle US government probe over DEI

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Parton as a “humanitarian hero,” “beloved queer icon,” feminist symbol, and advocate for marginalized communities, emphasizing poverty-to-success resilience and philanthropy; right-leaning accounts instead portray a “larger-than-life” Tennessee-rooted “American institution,” stressing faith, entrepreneurship, patriotism, and Trump’s mourning, including “in the arms of Jesus” and “tragic.” Center coverage de-emphasizes ideological cues, presenting a “rare celebrity” through career chronology and cautiously treating conflicting health or cancer claims.
The pivotal divide is whether her legacy signifies inclusion and progressive cultural alliance or Christian, national identity and individual achievement.
All perspectives nevertheless emphasize her music , six-decade career, charitable work, and exceptional cross-partisan popularity.
summary: On Tuesday, August 25, 2026, country music icon Dolly Parton died at age 80 at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville following a brief battle with cancer.
Parton's representatives confirmed the diagnosis was not previously public, clarifying the brief illness that led her to cancel a planned Las Vegas residency and other appearances.
A prolific artist and philanthropist, Parton sold more than 100 million records worldwide and founded the Imagination Library in 1995, which has provided nearly 308 million books to children.
President Donald Trump ordered American flags lowered nationwide for one week, while Parton's nephew Bryan Seaver announced her passing in a video, saying she "lived in the light."
Her estate and creative partners committed to maintaining her philanthropic projects, with an autobiographical Broadway musical scheduled to debut in December 2026, ensuring her legacy endures.
title: Dolly Parton Died After a ‘Brief Battle with Cancer,’ Her Team Confirms

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the incident as resistance to Trump-era enforcement, emphasizing Bovino as an “infamous” figure from an “aggressive immigration crackdown” and portraying “You’re not welcome here” as justified rejection.
Right-Leaning coverage foregrounds the “scary confrontation,” implying intimidation and asking “Why this bakery?” while de-emphasizing immigration-policy context.

summary: On Sunday, Manolo Betancur denied former U.S. Border Patrol Commander-at-Large Gregory Bovino entry to Manolo's Bakery in Charlotte. The confrontation occurred outside the business, which became a focal point during last year's federal immigration crackdown.

Led by Bovino, 'Operation Charlotte's Web' occurred last November, resulting in more than 370 arrests across North Carolina . The bakery temporarily closed during the operation, citing concerns for employees and customers.

Betancur estimated his bakery lost between $50,000 and $64,000 in revenue during the crackdown. He described the recent encounter as "tense," as the two discussed immigration enforcement and its impact on local families.

Bovino claimed on X he visited to argue that businesses "potentially hire and depend on" people in the country illegally "are flourishing." He doubled down, writing, "We gave them hell here in this place."
Advocating for immigrant communities, Betancur argues the enforcement tactics brought "hate to our city." He continues managing his businesses while addressing financial strain from the operation.
title: Charlotte Bakery Owner Denies Entry to Former Border Patrol Commander

summary: On Sunday, a 24-year-old Israeli man from Beitar Illit was moderately wounded in a stabbing attack near the village of Al-Auja in the Jordan Valley. He was evacuated to Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem.

The Israel Defense Forces launched a large-scale manhunt for the assailant, deploying Duvdevan commandos, the Nitzan 636 Unit, and Israeli Air Force assets. Roadblocks were established around Al-Auja and surrounding areas.

Magen David Adom medics Gal Shani and Shai Igner arrived at the scene and reported "considerable commotion" upon arrival. The victim remained fully conscious during evacuation to the hospital by intensive care ambulance.

Al-Auja sits along Route 90, a vital north-south highway in the Jordan Valley previously targeted by violence. In March 2024, a Palestinian gunman opened fire on vehicles and buses near the village, wounding three Israelis.

Data from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs shows 3,033 Israeli settler attacks across the West Bank between January 1, 2025, and June 31, 2026. This reflects broader regional security tensions.
title: One Wounded in Suspected Stabbing Attack in West Bank Town, IDF Investigating

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames *Naza* as an urgent exposé, using terms like “genocide,” “calculated mass killing,” and “hot-button” to amplify its accusation that Israeli systems deliberately target Palestinian civilians, while celebrating the filmmakers’ “Oscar win” and surprise competition entry.

Right-Leaning coverage de-emphasizes that allegation, stressing the “Oscar-winning team,” festival programming, and a recurring pattern of “highly charged” conflict films rather than endorsing the documentary’s conclusions.
Center coverage bridges the divide by describing the film as examining civilian deaths and explaining its military-derived title.

summary: On Monday, the Venice Film Festival added documentary 'NAZA' to its official competition at the 83rd edition, making it the only feature documentary among 21 films competing for the Golden Lion at the Sept. 10 premiere.

Directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature with 'No Other Land,' are returning with a new documentary about the war in Gaza about a year and a half after their Oscar victory.

The film's title 'NAZA' derives from a Hebrew military acronym for 'collateral damage'; shot at night on Tel Aviv rooftops, it is based on Abraham's investigations published between 2023 and 2025 in Local Call, +972 magazine and The Guardian.

Executive producer Jonathan Glazer, Oscar-winning director of 'The Zone of Interest,' joins producer James Wilson on the project, with the film screening Sept. 10 at 5:15 p.m. in the Sala Grande alongside the directors and Guardian journalists.

Last year, 'The Voice of Hind Rajab' won second prize at Venice with a record 23-minute standing ovation, marking the second consecutive year a Gaza-focused documentary has competed for the Golden Lion after international protests on the Lido.
title: Venice adds Gaza documentary by Oscar-winning team to main competition

Center coverage more cautiously foregrounds Governor Moore’s complaint about unannounced “sweeps.” All emphasize the two-week total, but the divide reflects broader disputes over federal power, public safety, and immigration.
summary: The Department of Homeland Security announced 1,328 arrests during 'Operation Safe Community- Washington, D.C.,' a two-week enforcement effort concluding August 14 across Washington, Virginia, and Maryland.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticized sanctuary policies in Virginia and Maryland, claiming they elevate illegal immigrants' needs above Americans' safety despite ICE executing the operation regardless.
Of the 1,328 arrested, nearly 400 have been convicted or charged with crimes in the United States; DHS reported members of MS-13, 18th Street Gang, and Tren de Aragua were apprehended.

Enforcement actions included arrests of individuals with histories of kidnapping, murder, and sexual assault; ICE apprehended alleged MS-13 member Mauricio Antonio Barrera-Navidad in Hyattsville, Maryland.

This effort follows a similar operation in Atlanta in July, which led to arrests of more than 1,200 undocumented immigrants across Georgia as authorities prioritize removing those with criminal histories.
title: ICE announces more than 1,300 arrests in Virginia, Maryland
